tier_reason: Test code is public (dft_simd.cpp, dft_simd_1024.cpp, dft_simd_1024_avx512.cpp, gtest cases against fftwf plans made with FFTW_MEASURE), CMakeLists.txt sets -O3 -march=native, and the 2018 runs name the compiler and CPU (Apple LLVM 9.0.0 on i5-5287U; gcc 4.8.5 on Xeon E5-2650 v4). The 2025 EPYC 9474F table names no compiler, so tier A rests on the 2018 runs.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 2025, AMD EPYC 9474F single core: 60-sample AVX2 codelet with fixed strides 79 ms vs FFTW aligned single-DFT plan 858 ms (10.8x per the README); 1024-sample AVX2 7,270 ms vs 12,136 ms (1.67x, derived from page data; README says about 1.6x) and AVX512 10,610 ms vs 24,657 ms (2.3x). 2018, MacBook Pro i5-5287U: 8-transform 60-sample codelet 379 ms vs best FFTW plan 1,912 ms (about 5x per the README) and 207 ms with compile-time strides. 2018, Xeon E5-2650 v4 with gcc 4.8.5: AVX codelet 220 ms vs best FFTW case 2,194 ms (a factor of 10 per the README).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: CMakeLists.txt adds -march=native and -O3 (also for RelWithDebInfo), C++11; README build uses -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithDebInfo. Apple LLVM 9.0.0 (clang-900.0.39.2) for the 2018 MacBook run and gcc 4.8.5 (Red Hat 4.8.5-16) for the Xeon E5-2650 v4 run; compiler for the 2025 EPYC run not stated; FFTW from MacPorts for the 2018 run, FFTW version and build not stated otherwise
corrections.workload: Bulk transformation of short single-precision real-to-complex DFTs: 2^24 (16.8 million) transforms of 60 samples in the original test and of 1024 samples in the 2025 AVX2 test, and 2^25 transforms of 1024 samples in the 2025 AVX512 test (nvec=16), with codelets generated by FFTW's genfft and compiled for AVX/AVX2/AVX512 vector types so that 8 (or 16) transforms run side by side ('vertical' SIMD). FFTW cases use fftwf_plan_dft_r2c_1d or fftwf_plan_many_dft_r2c with FFTW_MEASURE.
corrections.caveats: Author's own benchmark of a bulk short-DFT workload where FFTW's horizontal SIMD is inefficient, so it does not show a win on single large transforms. The test code fills the input directly in the interleaved SIMD layout before the loop and re-transforms the same in-cache buffer, so packing into and out of that layout is not timed; when FFTW is given the same interleaved layout (FFTW_Aligned_TransposedEight) it is slower than its own contiguous plans. Times appear to be gtest per-test durations, which would also count FFTW_MEASURE planning in the FFTW cases (small next to the totals). The AVX512 column runs twice as many transforms (2^25) as the AVX2 columns, so compare ratios only within a column. The 2025 EPYC table names no compiler or FFTW build. It is a test and demonstration repository rather than a packaged library; users generate codelets for their own sizes with genfft. GPL-2.0-or-later (source headers; LICENSE holds the GPLv2 text) inherited from FFTW codelet generators; the author notes copyright on machine-generated code is unclear; README text is CC-BY-SA-4.0.

notes: All quoted numbers match the README. License refined to GPL-2.0-or-later from the source headers. The AVX512 test runs 2^25 transforms (twice the AVX2 count), which explains its larger absolute times. The packing question in the record is resolved: data are pre-laid-out in SIMD form and packing is not timed.

tier_reason: BENCHMARKS.md is regenerated by public code (benchmarks/run.sh, benchmarks/cbench/fftw_bench.c, Go benchmarks) and states go1.26.4, FFTW 3.3.11 Homebrew NEON bottle with FFTW_MEASURE threads=1, and Apple M4 Max; the 2026-09-30 fresh runs add EPYC 7773X and Neoverse-N1 with FFTW 3.3.10 built from source, raw data in benchmarks/results/.

corrections.claimed_speedup: June snapshot tables (Apple M4 Max), go-fft vs FFTW: lags FFTW 1.17x to 3.28x on complex 1-D rows (e.g. N=1,024 3,395 ns vs 2,127 ns); faster only on the 2-D multicore rows: 256x256 208,437 ns vs 271,098 ns; 512x512 633,920 ns vs 1,247,215 ns; 1024x1024 2,784,623 ns vs 6,301,688 ns. Vs scipy.fft (pocketfft) complex 1-D: N=256 716 ns vs 2,302 ns; N=1,024 3,395 ns vs 4,470 ns; N=65,536 377,784 ns vs 499,500 ns (slower at N=1,048,576: 13.36 ms vs 8.04 ms). Summary of that snapshot: at or above parity with FFTW on 3 of 24 ops and with gonum on 19 of 19; 'typically 3-5x on composite N' faster than gonum. Fresh single-threaded 1-D runs of 2026-09-30 (go-fft time / FFTW time, below 1 = go-fft faster): complex 2^20 0.81 on M4 Max and 0.67 on Neoverse-N1; prime 1009 0.53 (M4 Max), 0.75 (EPYC 7773X), 0.54 (Neoverse-N1); RFFT 2^20 0.92 on Neoverse-N1; complex 65536 1.00 on Neoverse-N1; most other 1-D rows still lag 1.07x to 2.92x; 2-D 512^2/1024^2 multicore 0.43/0.45 (M4 Max), 1.63/0.87 (EPYC 7773X), 0.51/0.25 (Neoverse-N1).
corrections.hardware: Apple M4 Max (12P+4E), macOS 26.5, for the main tables; fresh 2026-09-30 runs also on AMD EPYC 7773X (Zen 3, GCC Compile Farm cfarm420, 128 threads) and ARM Neoverse-N1 (cfarm424, 64 cores)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: go1.26.4 (CGO=0 pure Go; cross-compiled for the Linux hosts), go test -benchtime=1s; FFTW 3.3.11 Homebrew arm64 bottle with NEON on the M4 Max and FFTW 3.3.10 built from source with SSE2/AVX/AVX2/FMA (Zen 3) or NEON (N1) on the Linux hosts, plans FFTW_MEASURE threads=1 from a C harness; numpy 2.5.0 and scipy 1.18.0 pinned single-threaded (2.5.3 / 1.18.1 on the Linux hosts)
corrections.caveats: Pure Go library, not callable from C++ without cgo; listed for the FFTW comparison. In the June M4 Max snapshot it does not beat FFTW on any single-threaded row; the fresh 2026-09-30 runs show single-threaded wins only at a few sizes (complex 2^20 on M4 Max and Neoverse-N1, prime N=1009 on all three hosts, RFFT 2^20 on N1), while most 1-D rows still lag FFTW by 1.07x to 2.92x and the M4 Max run was under background load (load average 3.4-5). The 2-D wins come from go-fft fanning rows and columns across goroutines while FFTW, numpy and scipy run single-threaded, so the 2-D comparison is not apples-to-apples; the 2-D fresh rows also predate a fan-out fix. FFT2/FFTN return a newly allocated slice, which the report says skews 2-D comparisons against FFTW on many-core hosts via GC cost. The README attributes part of the scipy gap at small N to Python FFI overhead, so the scipy comparison there is not like-for-like. The README tables still show the June snapshot. Very young repository (oldest commit on the first commits page 2026-06-20).

notes: June-snapshot numbers in the record match BENCHMARKS.md, but the file now also carries fresh 2026-09-30 three-host runs in which go-fft beats single-threaded FFTW at a few 1-D sizes, so the record's 'not faster than FFTW in 1-D' line was outdated and is corrected. Language is Go, so this is out of the C++ catalog's core scope; the orchestrator may prefer to file it as off-language.

tier_reason: astral4/fft-benchmark is independent but a small personal repo (5 stars), not a well-known suite, and its benches/fftw.rs builds a new FFTW_ESTIMATE plan inside every timed iteration (PhastFT and RustFFT also plan per iteration), so it measures one-shot plan-plus-execute rather than FFTW's execution speed. PhastFT's own steady-state benches (benches/fftw_lib/mod.rs, FFTW_MEASURE plan reused) are first-party, plots only, on an Apple M2 with no compiler version stated, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: astral4/fft-benchmark (M1 MacBook Pro, single thread, plan created inside each timed iteration for every library; forward times): f32 N=1024 4.749 us (PhastFT) vs 7.291 us (FFTW, FFTW_ESTIMATE); f32 N=1,048,576 10.21 ms vs 14.20 ms; f32 N=8,388,608 109.0 ms vs 193.3 ms (RustFFT 103.9 ms). Author's conclusion: 'phastft was the fastest in most tests, but rustfft was the fastest on the smallest and largest sequence lengths tested'; 'fftw was consistently slower than both rustfft and phastft'. PhastFT allocated about 5x less memory than RustFFT (derived from page data: 8.388 MB vs 41.94 MB at N=2^20 f32). PhastFT's own single-threaded criterion overlays (Apple M2, FFTW 3.3.8 via the fftw crate, plan reused) show FFTW_MEASURE at 1.31x to 2.04x PhastFT's time for f32 N=2^6 to 2^14 and 2.1x to 3.6x for f32 N=2^15 to 2^24, and 1.2x to 2.0x for f64 N=2^15 to 2^24 (derived from the bar labels in the SVG plots, which are relative to RustFFT).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: astral4 run: rustc 1.80.0-nightly (d2d24e395 2024-05-03), cargo bench profile with lto = true and default opt-level 3, no target-cpu (Cargo.toml); phastft v0.2.1, rustfft v6.2.0, fftw crate v0.8.0 over FFTW 3.3.8 compiled with Apple clang 15.0.0 (clang-1500.0.40.1); FFTW configure flags (e.g. NEON) not stated
corrections.hardware: M1 MacBook Pro (Apple M1; exact model not stated) for astral4; PhastFT's own plots use a MacBook Air with Apple M2, 4P+4E cores, 24 GB, macOS 26.4.1
corrections.caveats: The independent astral4 benchmark times plan creation inside every iteration for all three libraries and plans FFTW with FFTW_ESTIMATE, which explains FFTW's roughly 1.4 us floor at N=8; it is a one-shot (plan plus execute) comparison, not a measure of FFTW's steady-state execution. It is a small personal repo from 2024 benchmarking phastft v0.2.1, while the crate is now v0.4.1 with the parallel feature on by default. RustFFT beats PhastFT at N=16 and 32 and at N>=2^22 for f32, and at N=16, 32, 65,536 and N>=2^21 for f64. In PhastFT's own steady-state plots FFTW (3.3.8 built by the Rust fftw crate) is also 1.3x to 3.9x slower than RustFFT, which suggests that FFTW build lacks NEON codelets on Apple Silicon (inference, not stated anywhere), so the FFTW comparison on Apple Silicon should be treated with caution. PhastFT's README plots are multi-threaded vs single-threaded RustFFT and FFTW3; numbers appear only as plot bar labels. Rust library, power-of-two lengths only. The QuState/PhastFT URL redirects to smu160/PhastFT.
